source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Bird) Thomas Kuhn
finding: Kuhn's cycle: pre-paradigm, normal science, anomaly, crisis, revolution, new normal science. Anomalies pile up; only the troublesome ones undermine normal science.
numbers: Five phases; crisis cited at Kuhn 1962/1970, pp. 66-76.
limits: Secondary summary, not Kuhn's text. Kuhn's own book was not opened.
agent_relevance: S6 idea: a frame is dropped after accumulated failures, not after one.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Bird) Thomas Kuhn
finding: Crisis is a broad loss of confidence in the practice, not one refuting result. Popper needs one reproducible anomaly; Kuhn does not. Normal science neither tests nor tries to confirm its guiding theory and explains anomalies away where it can.
limits: The article gives no count of how many anomalies make a crisis; Kuhn gives none.
agent_relevance: A trigger of N independent failures is our design; Kuhn gives no N. Mark the threshold [D].

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Bird) Thomas Kuhn
finding: Puzzle-solving is the normal-science mode: the solver expects a decent chance of success, relies on personal skill and familiar methods. This is why normal science accumulates and revolution does not.
agent_relevance: Inside a frame, the agent should treat failures as puzzles (fix and continue), not as signs of a wrong frame, until the signal pattern changes.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Bird) Thomas Kuhn
finding: Theory choice rests on five shared values: accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, fruitfulness. They are imprecise and can conflict, so they do not fix a choice alone. Kuhn: the values let rational men disagree.
numbers: Five criteria (Kuhn 1977, pp. 321-2).
limits: Values are not an algorithm.
agent_relevance: The agent's choice between old and new frame can use these five as a fixed checklist scored in code, with no weighting claim.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Bird) Thomas Kuhn
finding: Incommensurability has methodological, observational and semantic forms, and Kuhn said it does not mean non-comparability. The 1970 postscript answered Masterman by reading paradigm as exemplar and disciplinary matrix.
numbers: Three forms of incommensurability.
limits: Masterman's count of senses of paradigm is not in the SEP page; not verified here.
agent_relevance: A new frame cannot be scored in the old frame's terms alone; judge on held-out outcomes (G3), not on the old frame's vocabulary.

source: Wikipedia: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
finding: Publication facts and reception. Over one million copies sold; reported in 1987 as the most-cited 20th-century book in arts and humanities for 1976-1983.
numbers: 264 pages; first edition 1962; second edition 1970 with postscript; 50th anniversary edition 2012.
quote: As a paradigm is stretched to its limits, anomalies … accumulate.
limits: Wikipedia, secondary. Citation figure is the page's report of a 1987 ranking.
agent_relevance: Shows how well known the theory is; says nothing on its evidential support.

source: Wikipedia: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
finding: Scientists keep faith in the paradigm until a credible alternative is available, however many anomalies remain. Critics: Toulmin said revision is more common inside normal science than Kuhn allows; Hanson called the theory circular and unfalsifiable; Feyerabend said normal science fits organised crime too.
limits: The page read covers only the first 100,000 characters. No empirical test of the theory is listed on the page.
agent_relevance: Design point: an alternative frame must exist before the old one is dropped. S6 should build the candidate frame first, then compare.

source: Bruner & Postman (1949) On the perception of incongruity: a paradigm
finding: Founding psychology demonstration often tied to Kuhn. 28 Harvard and Radcliffe students saw playing cards by tachistoscope, some with colour and suit reversed. Trick cards needed about four times the exposure of normal cards.
numbers: N=28. Exposures 10 ms up to 1000 ms. Recognition = two successive correct reports. Normal-card mean threshold 28 ms; incongruous 114 ms (t=3.76, p<.01). 100% of normal cards recognised by 350 ms; 89.7% of incongruous at 1000 ms.
limits: Tiny, old, student sample; no pre-registration. Kuhn cited this study in his book (from memory, not verified this session); the 1949 paper itself does not cite Kuhn.
agent_relevance: Shows a prior frame can block seeing the odd item; the agent should read failing outputs literally (G2).

source: Bruner & Postman (1949) On the perception of incongruity: a paradigm
finding: Reaction types before recognition: dominance (seeing the expected card), compromise, disruption, then recovery.
numbers: Dominance 27 of 28 subjects (96%) on trick cards vs 2 of 28 on normal. Compromise 50% of subjects on trick red cards vs 15% on normal red. Disruption 16 of 28 (57%), about 4% of pre-recognition responses. Six subjects kept dominance responses over 50 exposures up to 1000 ms without recognising the card; runs of 24, 44 and 16 successive wrong responses.
limits: Counts come from the authors' coding; no inter-rater figure was seen.
agent_relevance: Persistent wrong-frame responses can run very long; a stuck count (same error repeated) is a usable trigger.

source: Bruner & Postman (1949) On the perception of incongruity: a paradigm
finding: Exposure to incongruity speeds later recognition: thresholds fall with prior trick cards, so a few clashes weaken the expectation.
numbers: Incongruous-card threshold 360 ms with no prior cards; 420 ms after normal cards (not significant); 230 ms after one trick card; 84 ms after two or three trick cards.
quote: Correct recognition results when inappropriate expectancies are discarded after failure of confirmation.
limits: Thresholds as reported in the text; the figure with per-exposure percentages was not available.
agent_relevance: Supports a counting rule: one clash changes little, 2-3 clashes change a lot. Our S6 N of 2-3 independent failures has a rough analogue here.

source: Horner & Tung (2011) replication of Bruner & Postman (as reported in a search snippet)
finding: A reported replication found mixed results and said its findings were inconsistent with an interpretation of resistance to incongruities.
numbers: Not read; numbers unknown.
limits: Not opened (page returned 403). Details come from a search summary only. Treat as unverified until read.
agent_relevance: Do not rest the prior-frame-blocks-perception claim on B&P alone.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) Factors that influence how people respond to anomalous data (CogSci)
finding: Taxonomy: faced with anomalous data a person holding theory A can (1) ignore, (2) reject it, (3) exclude it from the theory's domain, (4) hold it in abeyance, (5) reinterpret it, (6) change the theory peripherally, (7) change the theory. Only the last is Kuhn-style change.
numbers: Seven responses.
limits: Taxonomy is theoretical; the sample experiment uses one domain (Cretaceous extinction).
agent_relevance: An agent has the same seven escapes: ignore, blame the tool, call it out of scope, defer, reinterpret, patch, replace. A schema can log which one it used.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) Factors that influence how people respond to anomalous data (CogSci)
finding: Entrenched theories give theory-preserving responses. Undergraduates read a meteor-impact account with extensive or minimal support, then two anomalous data and an alternative theory; the well-supported version was less likely to change (reported from Chinn & Brewer 1992). Burbules and Linn (1988): students kept a wrong rule after anomalous data and changed only when told the correct principle.
numbers: Numbers for the 1992 study are not given in this text.
limits: Secondary report of earlier work inside this paper.
agent_relevance: More support for a frame means more resistance; a long successful run in one frame should raise the bar for noticing it fails (guard against sunk-frame inertia).

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) Factors that influence how people respond to anomalous data (CogSci)
finding: Experiment: 64 undergraduates, 2x2 (alternative theory available or not, data weak or strong). Surprising null results: the alternative theory changed neither data evaluation nor later belief, and the strong data did not change ratings.
numbers: N=64. Belief drop in meteor theory after anomaly: .97 with alternative vs .72 without (F<1). Belief in data 5.4 vs 5.6 (weak vs strong, F<1). 7 of the 16 who rejected the strong data attacked one of its two independent lines and ignored the other.
limits: Students had little stake in the Cretaceous question; the authors say this may be why an alternative theory did not matter. Cuts against the simple claim that an alternative is needed.
agent_relevance: Competing result: an available alternative did not change behaviour here. Our S6 should test this, not assume it.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) Factors that influence how people respond to anomalous data (CogSci)
finding: Data evaluation is strongly theory-laden: proponents of the rival volcano theory rated the same data as far more believable than proponents of the meteor theory.
numbers: Believability 12 vs 5.1 as printed (t(40)=2.48, p<.02). Accepted the data: 6 of 10 volcano proponents vs 4 of 32 meteor proponents (p<.01). The other 28 rejected or reinterpreted it.
limits: The 12 as printed is on a 0-10 scale in the text, so it may be a typo or a sum; read with care.
agent_relevance: Same output read differently under different frames: a judge must not know the favoured frame (G5).

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) Factors that influence how people respond to anomalous data (CogSci)
finding: Data are not wholly theory-laden: how much a person discounted the data (belief times inconsistency) still predicted belief change after controlling for prior belief.
numbers: Discount measure vs belief change r=-.46 (p<.001); regression delta R2=.25, F(1,63)=23.66. Believing the data alone r=-.24 and inconsistency alone r=-.27, both not reliable.
limits: Correlational.
agent_relevance: Accepting a failure as a real failure (not noise) is the step that moves belief; make the agent record that decision explicitly.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) Factors that influence how people respond to anomalous data (CogSci)
finding: Features of data that favour theory change: credibility of the source, low ambiguity, many lines of evidence. Stavy's iodine versus acetone case: blue iodine gas was visible, so students accepted mass conservation; colourless acetone was not.
numbers: Acetone vs iodine difference is described, no numbers. Reasons for rejecting data fell into five categories among 33 subjects.
limits: The text says there is little empirical research on multiple lines of evidence.
agent_relevance: Independent failure signals (different tests, different seeds) are stronger than repeats of one test; this supports several independent failures as the trigger.

source: Dunbar (1997) How scientists think: on-line creativity and conceptual change in science
finding: In vivo study: one year in four molecular biology and immunology labs; weekly lab meetings were the main source of new ideas and were recorded. Meetings gave a better record of idea change than interviews or notebooks.
numbers: 4 labs; 16 meetings coded for analogy; first 4 months spent on familiarisation.
limits: Small number of labs, one author's coding, details anonymised.
agent_relevance: Records made at the time beat later recall; log failures as they happen.

source: Dunbar (1997) How scientists think: on-line creativity and conceptual change in science
finding: Unexpected findings are common, and scientists attend to them rather than explaining them away.
numbers: Lab A, 4 meetings, 6 experiments, 70 conditions: 22 expected, 18 unexpected, 30 exploratory. Group interactions: 23 for expected findings vs 176 for unexpected. Of 18 unexpected, 8 were consistent with the hypothesis and 10 inconsistent.
limits: One lab; Dunbar also notes that subjects in his own earlier lab tasks ignored unexpected results.
agent_relevance: Counter to Kuhn's picture of explaining anomalies away: in real labs surprise draws more reasoning. A trigger can start inquiry, not only replacement.

source: Dunbar (1997) How scientists think: on-line creativity and conceptual change in science
finding: Whether surprise is attended to depends on timing and on what it contradicts. Early and about an auxiliary hypothesis: ignored. Early and about a core assumption: focused on. Late in the project: attended whatever it touches.
numbers: Qualitative finding from new analyses; no counts given.
limits: Described as analyses in progress; not a full test.
agent_relevance: Separate failures that hit core assumptions from those that hit setup details; only core ones count toward a frame switch.

source: Dunbar (1997) How scientists think: on-line creativity and conceptual change in science
finding: Groups catch reasoning errors: other lab members limited, expanded, replaced or discarded the inductions of the presenter.
numbers: HIV lab talk: 5 sets of findings, 11 inductions, 7 modified or dropped by others. 30% of inductions and deductions shared by more than one person; 12% had more than two participants.
limits: Single talk plus a lab-wide claim of ubiquity; no statistics.
agent_relevance: A second agent with a different view can play the group role, but G4 says same-model samples are not independent.

source: Dunbar (1997) How scientists think: on-line creativity and conceptual change in science
finding: A conceptual change case: a surprising result (both B-cell types found in heart and joints) led through rounds of group reasoning to two new mechanisms replacing one assumed mechanism. Analogies were local, not distant.
numbers: 99 analogies across 16 meetings (mean 6.1, range 2-14); 40 within organism, 57 other organism, 2 non-biological; the post-doc could not recall the online analogies at 1, 3 or 9 months.
limits: One anonymised case with names and mechanisms changed.
agent_relevance: Change came from one clear surprise plus talk, not from a long pile-up of anomalies: evidence against a pure accumulation trigger.

source: Wikipedia: Paul Thagard (explanatory coherence, ECHO)
finding: Thagard modelled conceptual revolutions with explanatory coherence: propositions linked by positive and negative constraints, split into accepted and rejected sets that satisfy the most constraint weight. Applied to the chemical revolution (1990) and set out in Conceptual Revolutions (1992).
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: The Wikipedia page does not mention ECHO by name or Kuhn. Critics (seen in a search result, not opened) say ECHO reconstructs the debate from the winner's view.
agent_relevance: Frame choice as constraint satisfaction in code (G5) matches our design: accept the frame set with higher coherence on held-out evidence.

source: Sterman (1985) A behavioral model of the economic and scientific revolutions; Wittenberg & Sterman (1999) dynamic model of scientific paradigms
finding: System dynamics models of the Kuhn cycle. Confidence in the paradigm falls when anomalies exceed an acceptable level or puzzle-solving progress slows. Later versions have competing paradigms and path dependence.
numbers: Not read (PDF blocked, archive page was a bot check). No parameter values known.
limits: Description comes from a search summary only. Unverified.
agent_relevance: Closest formal match to an S6 trigger: a stock of confidence with anomaly count and progress rate as inputs. Read the primary before use.

source: Schapiro, Black & Varshney (2025) Transformational creativity in science: a graphical theory
finding: Formalises a scientific conceptual space as a directed acyclic graph where sink nodes are axioms and other nodes are rules. Proves that changing axioms has the most transformative potential, and maps Kuhn's puzzle solving, crisis and revolution onto it.
numbers: Three historical cases tabulated: Ptolemaic to heliocentric, Newtonian to relativistic, Euclidean to non-Euclidean geometry. No empirical test.
quote: It's as if the scientific community has been transported to another planet
limits: Short theory paper, no data, no LLM experiments.
agent_relevance: A frame switch should change root assumptions (axioms), not rewrite surface rules. Reframing prompts can name the assumption being dropped.

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: what does the scientific method buy an LLM agent?
finding: A Kuhn agent was added to an LLM loop for DNA motif discovery. It fires after a configurable number of consecutive non-improving iterations, gets the task without the history file, and receives an injected assumption plus a cross-discipline inspiration.
numbers: Kuhn agent: 63 runs, 33.5M tokens, 531K tokens per run, 3 days (of 2,151 runs and 229.0M tokens in total). Phase 1 stalled at 0.664 after 49 straight runs with no accepted improvement; Phase 2 reached 0.846 in 10 days.
limits: The paper says its ablation negated this structure as non-load bearing; no arm isolates the Kuhn agent. The big Phase 2 gain came from infrastructure fixes made at the same time.
agent_relevance: Direct test of switching frame after failures: evidence is weak and the paper says it did not matter. Fresh context without history is the part worth testing.

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: what does the scientific method buy an LLM agent?
finding: Ten preregistered ablation arms against one-shot bandit nulls. Seven of ten loop arms did not beat drawing fresh samples; the full scaffold scored below blind sampling at 7-8 times the tokens; a floor prompt with no framework won.
numbers: Bandit pool H n=114, mean 0.7644, E[best-of-15]=0.8463; HG n=88, mean 0.7802, E[best-of-15]=0.8455. Floor prompt L 0.8896 at the common horizon vs full scaffold B 0.7942 (n=10 per arm). Full scaffold used 111.4M tokens per run vs 15M for fifteen pulls.
limits: Single task family (DNA motifs); one independent author; on a held-out set loop and bandit agreed within 0.002.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: elaborate reframing machinery may cost more than it gives. Test S6 against plain resampling before keeping it.

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: what does the scientific method buy an LLM agent?
finding: A framing-only rung (paradigm framing text, no persistent state) gave the best held-out draw, but its proxy peak was low and its other draws were far below.
numbers: r5 1: proxy peak 0.8364, held-out 0.8819 (Full TF Metric) and 0.8964 (STREME benchmark). Late proxy-saturated artifacts transferred at 0.58-0.60.
limits: Best-of-draw selection; the same rung's other draws were far below.
agent_relevance: Reframing may raise variance more than mean; keep selection in code on held-out data (G3).

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: an iterative planning and search approach to enhance novelty and diversity of LLM generated ideas
finding: Nova uses ten scientific-discovery methods as prompts; one is Scientific Paradigm Shift (identify accumulated anomalies and crises, develop new conceptual frameworks) and another is Explaining and Integrating Anomalous Findings. Kuhn is the stated theory base.
numbers: Iterative planning gave 3.4 times more unique novel ideas than baseline; 170 seed papers; Swiss tournament scored by an LLM ranker.
limits: The Kuhn-based prompts are not ablated one by one in the parts read. Success is judged by LLM and human ratings of novelty, not correctness.
agent_relevance: Evidence that Kuhn prompts have been used, not that they help. No anomaly counter is used.

source: Wikipedia: Research program (Lakatos)
finding: Lakatos: a hard core immune to revision, a malleable protective belt. Programs are progressive if they predict new facts and degenerating if they lose that momentum, and can recover. Many programs coexist, unlike Kuhn's single paradigm.
limits: Page omits heuristics and Laudan.
agent_relevance: A better trigger than failure count alone: is the current frame still predicting new checkable things (progress) or only patching (degeneration)?

source: Aerts & Aerts Arguelles (2022) Human perception as a phenomenon of quantization
finding: Uses the Bruner-Postman cards as an example of reconciling a top-down expectation with a bottom-up stimulus and describes the dominance reaction.
numbers: No new data; a quantum-style model.
limits: Not a test of Kuhn; repeats the 1949 design (five cards, one to four incongruous).
agent_relevance: Minor: the 1949 setup is still used as a template for expectation-versus-stimulus conflict.
